transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Mostly I’m here because I’m just… tired. Not normal tired, I guess. It’s like this heavy, drained feeling that doesn’t really go away even if I sleep. I’ll think, okay, if I just get a full night or rest for a day, I’ll feel better, but then I still wake up feeling like I’m already behind somehow.

And it’s making regular things feel weirdly hard. Like unloading the dishwasher can feel like this whole project I have to talk myself into, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud. Or I’ll sit down to read for this certificate class I’m trying to work on, and I’ll get through a little bit and just feel like I can’t keep going, like my brain and body both hit a wall. So… yeah, that’s the main reason I came in. I’m tired in a way I can’t seem to fix.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, “depressed” feels like a big word, and I don’t know if what I’m feeling counts as that or if it’s more just being worn out and kind of weighed down. I wouldn’t say I’m walking around crying all the time or anything like that, but I also don’t feel like myself exactly.

It’s more like… everything has this dullness to it, I guess. Like I’m trying to do the normal things I should be able to do, and they just feel harder than they should. So maybe that is feeling down? I don’t know. I’m not trying to dodge the question, I just don’t really have a clean answer.
After physical or mental activity, do you feel significantly worse afterward?

Yeah, I think so. It’s not always dramatic like I collapse afterward, but even pretty normal things can take more out of me than they should. Like if I unload the dishwasher or try to sit and read for my certificate class, afterward I can feel like I’ve used up way more energy than that should require.

And it’s frustrating because I keep thinking, “Okay, just rest, just sleep, you’ll reset,” but sleep doesn’t really fix it. I can do something small and then feel like I need to recover from it, which makes me feel kind of ridiculous, because these aren’t huge physical tasks or anything. It’s just this tiredness that lingers and gets worse when I try to push through.
When you wake up after a full night of sleep, do you usually feel refreshed?

No, not really. That’s actually one of the more frustrating parts, because I’ll think, “Okay, I got a full night, so tomorrow should be better,” and then I wake up and it’s like… I don’t feel restored. I might technically have slept, but I still feel heavy and drained, almost like I’m starting the day already used up.

And then even small things feel bigger than they should. Like unloading the dishwasher can feel like this whole task I have to gear myself up for, or reading for my certificate class starts out okay and then suddenly feels like too much. So, no, I wouldn’t say I usually wake up refreshed, even if I slept enough hours.
Has this exhaustion been going on for six months or longer?

No, I don’t think it’s been six months. It feels long, honestly, because when you’re in it every day it kind of stretches out, but if I’m trying to be accurate, this quieter, low-energy stretch has been more like about three months.

That’s when I started noticing that I wasn’t just tired from a bad week or needing a weekend to catch up. It was more like my interest in things got lower and this heavy fatigue settled in and didn’t really lift the way I expected it to. So… not six months or longer, but definitely a few months. Maybe around three.
For the past few months, have you felt sad or down most of the day nearly every day?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve definitely felt… low, I guess, or kind of weighed down at times, but “sad most of the day nearly every day” feels harder for me to say yes to.

It’s not like I’m crying all day or constantly thinking, “I’m sad.” A lot of the time it’s more like I feel flat, or slowed down, or just not very bright inside, if that makes sense. But then there are also parts of the day where I’m distracted or just going through the motions, and I don’t know if that counts as feeling sad or not.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say it’s been clearly sad all day every day, but something has definitely felt off emotionally for the past few months.
Over the past few months, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… yes, I think that’s probably the clearest part of it, honestly. I’ve sort of stopped caring about the things that usually make me feel like me.

Like, I used to sketch pretty regularly—not necessarily anything amazing, just little studies or ideas in a notebook—and normally that feels grounding. But lately the sketchbook just sits there, and I’ll look at it and think I should want to pick it up, but I don’t. Same with going to gallery openings. That used to be something I’d actually get excited about, even just getting dressed and wandering around and seeing what people were making. Now it feels like this whole effort, and I can’t really imagine enjoying it once I’m there.

Cooking has been like that too. I used to like trying recipes or making something nice for myself, and now it’s more like… I don’t care enough. Yoga feels similar. And even tennis with a friend, which should be fun and social and active, just doesn’t pull me in the way it normally would.

So, yes. It’s not that I hate those things now, exactly. It’s more like the part of me that used to feel interested or pleased by them has gotten really quiet.
Over the past few months, has your appetite changed?

Yeah, it has. Not in a dramatic way where I’m, like, deliberately not eating or anything, but my appetite has been pretty off.

Some days I’ll get to later in the afternoon and realize I’ve basically only had coffee and maybe a few bites of something—like half a piece of toast or a couple forkfuls of leftovers—and I didn’t even really notice I was skipping meals. Food just doesn’t sound that appealing, or it feels like too much effort to decide what to eat.

And I have noticed my jeans are looser. I wasn’t trying to lose weight, so that kind of stood out to me. It’s not something I was aiming for; it just sort of happened along with not eating very much some days.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I’ve had clear thoughts like, “I’m going to hurt myself,” if that’s what you mean. And I don’t have, like, a plan or anything I’m sitting with.

But the “life isn’t worth living” part is harder, because sometimes when I’m really low or just worn out, I’ll have this kind of vague feeling of, “What is the point of doing all of this?” Not in a dramatic way, more like this heavy, exhausted thought that everything feels like too much. Then it passes, or I distract myself, or I just sort of keep going.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t been actively trying to hurt myself. But I have had those darker, pointless-feeling thoughts around the edges sometimes, if that makes sense.
Have you been moving or speaking more slowly than usual lately?

Yeah… I think so. Not every single day, but on the slower days it’s pretty noticeable to me.

It’s like my body is moving through wet cement, if that makes sense. I’ll be doing something basic, like getting up from the couch or walking to the kitchen, and everything just feels heavier and slower than it should. Not painful, exactly, just like there’s this delay between deciding to move and actually moving.

And talking can feel that way too. My spouse will ask me something simple, like what I want to do or whether I need anything, and I’ll just sit there for a weirdly long time trying to answer. I can tell it’s taking too long, which makes me feel awkward, but it’s like the words don’t come out right away. I’m not trying to ignore them. It’s more like everything in me is lagging.
Have you been feeling unusually sensitive to cold lately?

Um… unusually sensitive to cold? I don’t think so. I mean, I get cold sometimes, but not in a way that’s stood out to me as different or weird.

Like, I’ll put on a sweatshirt if the house is chilly, but I haven’t been thinking, “Why am I freezing all the time?” or anything like that. I guess I haven’t really been tracking it closely, but no, nothing noticeable comes to mind.
Before this started about three months ago, have you ever had another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in things most days?

I’m not sure, honestly. I’ve had low stretches before, like times where I felt really discouraged or kind of flat, but I don’t know if I could say it was a full two weeks most days, if that makes sense.

I’m trying to think back, and it all gets a little blurry because I don’t usually mark it on a calendar or anything. I can remember bad days, or maybe a bad week here and there, but whether it was really depressed or not interested in things nearly every day for two weeks… I don’t know that I can confidently say yes.

So I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not sure. Nothing as clear in my memory as, “that was definitely a two-week period.”
Before this current stretch, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I know you just asked that in a slightly different way, and I’m trying not to over-answer it, but… I really don’t know.

Before this current stretch, I’ve definitely had times where I felt down or kind of emotionally shut off, like I wasn’t as interested in things as I normally would be. But when you say nearly every day for at least two weeks, that’s the part I can’t honestly pin down. I can remember patches of feeling bad, but I don’t know if they lasted that long or if it was more like a few bad days mixed in with some okay days.

I don’t want to say yes just because I’ve had rough periods, if that makes sense. This one feels more clear to me because it’s recent and I’ve been aware of it. The older stuff is just harder for me to sort out. So… maybe there were times like that, but I’m not confident enough to say there definitely were.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or irritable for several days in a row?

Yeah… yes, I think so. There have been times where for weeks I felt almost, I don’t know, lit up. Like everything suddenly seemed possible and I was completely sure things were about to be amazing, even if nothing had really changed enough to explain why I felt that way.

And it wasn’t just being in a good mood for a day or two. It felt bigger than that, like I had this energy or excitement running through me. But at the same time, I could get really touchy. My husband would make some small comment about the budget, or something around the house, and I’d just snap at him like he had said something terrible. Then later I’d think, why did I react that strongly?

So yes, there have been periods like that, and they lasted more than several days. More like weeks, at least the ones I’m thinking of.
During those weeks when you felt lit up, did you need less sleep than usual?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I’m trying to think about those weeks specifically, and I don’t have a clean memory of, like, “Oh yes, I was only sleeping three hours and felt fine,” or anything that clear.

I do remember feeling more awake or keyed up in general during those times, but whether I actually needed less sleep than usual… I don’t know. I might have stayed up later some nights because I felt like my mind was still going, but I can’t confidently say my sleep was dramatically reduced or that I didn’t feel tired afterward.

So I guess the honest answer is: maybe a little, but I didn’t track it, and it’s not one of the things I remember clearly.
During those weeks when you felt lit up, were you more driven than usual to start or do a lot of projects or activities?

Yes. That part I remember pretty clearly, actually. I would suddenly feel like I had this whole plan for my life and I needed to act on all of it immediately.

Like, I started contacting galleries, and I was drafting sections for a newsletter, and then I was planning these community workshop ideas, and at the same time trying to line up freelance clients. It wasn’t just one project where I was excited and focused — it was like five different directions at once, and they all felt urgent and totally realistic in the moment.

Looking back, it was way more than I could actually follow through on. I’d start making lists and sending emails and sketching out plans, and I’d feel like, “Okay, this is it, I’m finally getting everything moving.” But then there was just too much happening, and a lot of it didn’t really get finished or went nowhere because I had taken on more than I could manage. So yes, definitely more driven than usual.
During those weeks when you felt lit up, did you feel more confident or powerful than usual?

Yes, I did. I don’t think I would have called it “powerful” at the time, because that sounds so dramatic, but… I definitely felt unusually sure of myself. Like I had finally figured out something everyone else hadn’t, or like I was suddenly capable of making these huge things happen if I just pushed hard enough.

I remember honestly believing I could take the newsletter idea, get a gallery partnership going, and turn that into some kind of consulting business or bigger professional thing almost overnight. And I mean, looking back, I hadn’t really worked out the basics. I didn’t have a clear business plan, or enough contacts, or even a realistic sense of how all of it would actually function. But at the time it didn’t feel unrealistic. It felt obvious, like, “Of course I can do this. Why wouldn’t this work?”

It wasn’t just normal confidence, I guess. It was more like this certainty that I was on the edge of something big and that I could pull it all together faster than anyone would expect. I felt kind of unstoppable in that way, even though now I can see there were a lot of missing pieces.
During those weeks when you felt lit up, did that cause serious problems in your life?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it catastrophic, but it definitely caused problems. More than I wanted to admit at the time.

The biggest thing is that I couldn’t actually keep everything organized. I’d have all these plans and ideas and I’d be starting things, but the normal stuff in my life started slipping. I fell behind in my certificate coursework because I kept thinking I was going to catch up later, or I’d sit down to do it and get pulled into some other plan that felt more urgent. And then suddenly I was behind enough that it felt embarrassing to even look at it.

At home, things piled up too. Bills, meals, basic household tasks — not because I didn’t care, but because I was just not following through consistently. I’d have these bursts where I thought I was going to reorganize everything, and then somehow the actual practical things didn’t get done. My spouse had to step in more, and I feel bad about that because it wasn’t fair. It put more on them.

And socially, I kind of pulled back from people and from art commitments I normally really care about. Which is strange, because I felt like I was doing all these big important things, but in reality I was dropping the regular things and relationships that keep me steady.

So yes, it did cause problems. I guess “serious” depends how you define it, but it affected my schoolwork, my home life, and my relationships enough that I can’t really say it was just harmless energy.
Did any of those unusually energized or lit-up periods last at least one full week?

Yes. It wasn’t just a day or two where I was in a good mood or had a burst of motivation. It lasted for weeks at a time, that kind of lit-up feeling where everything seemed exciting and possible and like it was all about to turn into something amazing.

I remember being really sure of myself during those stretches, like things were finally clicking and I just had to keep moving with it. But it wasn’t only upbeat, exactly. I could get irritable too, especially at home. If my husband made a small comment about the budget or the house, things that were probably reasonable to bring up, I’d snap at him like he was trying to slow me down or criticize me. At the time it felt like he was being negative, but looking back, my reaction was bigger than the comment deserved.

So yes, definitely at least a full week. More like several weeks, from what I remember.
During those lit-up periods, did you ever have beliefs that other people said were clearly untrue or unrealistic?

Yeah… I think so. Not like I believed something completely impossible in a bizarre way, but I definitely believed things that other people thought were unrealistic. At the time, I didn’t experience them as unrealistic at all.

The main one was this whole idea that I could take the newsletter I was working on, connect it with a gallery partnership, and somehow turn that into a consulting business or this much bigger professional thing almost immediately. Like, almost overnight, in my mind. I was talking about it as if it was just a matter of pushing hard enough and making the right moves, and then it would all fall into place.

And people around me were kind of trying to point out that I hadn’t really figured out the basics. I didn’t have a real plan, or enough contacts, or a clear sense of how the money would work, or what I was actually offering. But when they said that, I remember feeling like they just didn’t understand the scale of it yet. Like they were being too cautious or small-minded.

Looking back, it feels embarrassing, because there were so many steps missing. But at the time, I honestly believed I could make it into something big very quickly, and I was really certain about it.

doctor.intent: Open the interview by understanding the patient's main concern in their own words
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I’m here because I’m tired in a way that sleep doesn’t fix, like even unloading the dishwasher or reading for my certificate class can feel like too much.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I should return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S029.

patient.answer:
Mostly I’m here because I’m just… tired. Not normal tired, I guess. It’s like this heavy, drained feeling that doesn’t really go away even if I sleep. I’ll think, okay, if I just get a full night or rest for a day, I’ll feel better, but then I still wake up feeling like I’m already behind somehow.

And it’s making regular things feel weirdly hard. Like unloading the dishwasher can feel like this whole project I have to talk myself into, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud. Or I’ll sit down to read for this certificate class I’m trying to work on, and I’ll get through a little bit and just feel like I can’t keep going, like my brain and body both hit a wall. So… yeah, that’s the main reason I came in. I’m tired in a way I can’t seem to fix.

inference.note: Initial broad differential for persistent fatigue and low energy includes depressive disorders, dysthymia, neurasthenia/chronic fatigue-like presentations, and possible medical causes such as hypothyroidism.

doctor.intent: Assess depressed mood to distinguish depressive disorders from primarily physical-fatigue conditions like neurasthenia, chronic fatigue syndrome, or hypothyroidism.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about feeling down or depressed mood, but the symptom profile does not include a depressed mood item.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, “depressed” feels like a big word, and I don’t know if what I’m feeling counts as that or if it’s more just being worn out and kind of weighed down. I wouldn’t say I’m walking around crying all the time or anything like that, but I also don’t feel like myself exactly.

It’s more like… everything has this dullness to it, I guess. Like I’m trying to do the normal things I should be able to do, and they just feel harder than they should. So maybe that is feeling down? I don’t know. I’m not trying to dodge the question, I just don’t really have a clean answer.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fatigue is characterized by post-exertional worsening, which would help distinguish chronic fatigue syndrome from depressive and dysthymic disorders.
doctor.question: After physical or mental activity, do you feel significantly worse afterward?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I’m here because I’m tired in a way that sleep doesn’t fix, like even unloading the dishwasher or reading for my certificate class can feel like too much.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether activity worsens the patient's exhaustion, which most directly relates to persistent fatigue and lack of energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. It’s not always dramatic like I collapse afterward, but even pretty normal things can take more out of me than they should. Like if I unload the dishwasher or try to sit and read for my certificate class, afterward I can feel like I’ve used up way more energy than that should require.

And it’s frustrating because I keep thinking, “Okay, just rest, just sleep, you’ll reset,” but sleep doesn’t really fix it. I can do something small and then feel like I need to recover from it, which makes me feel kind of ridiculous, because these aren’t huge physical tasks or anything. It’s just this tiredness that lingers and gets worse when I try to push through.

inference.note: Post-exertional worsening and nonrestorative sleep strengthen G93.3; depressive disorders, neurasthenia, and hypothyroidism remain possible because low mood is still unclear and fatigue can overlap.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has unrefreshing sleep, which would strongly support chronic fatigue syndrome over depressive and thyroid-related causes.
doctor.question: When you wake up after a full night of sleep, do you usually feel refreshed?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I’m here because I’m tired in a way that sleep doesn’t fix, like even unloading the dishwasher or reading for my certificate class can feel like too much.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether sleep is restorative; this directly matches fatigue that is not relieved by rest.

patient.answer:
No, not really. That’s actually one of the more frustrating parts, because I’ll think, “Okay, I got a full night, so tomorrow should be better,” and then I wake up and it’s like… I don’t feel restored. I might technically have slept, but I still feel heavy and drained, almost like I’m starting the day already used up.

And then even small things feel bigger than they should. Like unloading the dishwasher can feel like this whole task I have to gear myself up for, or reading for my certificate class starts out okay and then suddenly feels like too much. So, no, I wouldn’t say I usually wake up refreshed, even if I slept enough hours.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the fatigue has persisted for at least six months, which helps distinguish chronic fatigue syndrome from depression, dysthymia, neurasthenia, or hypothyroidism.
doctor.question: Has this exhaustion been going on for six months or longer?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The quieter depressed stretch, with low interest and heavy fatigue, has been going on for about three months.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think it’s been six months. It feels long, honestly, because when you’re in it every day it kind of stretches out, but if I’m trying to be accurate, this quieter, low-energy stretch has been more like about three months.

That’s when I started noticing that I wasn’t just tired from a bad week or needing a weekend to catch up. It was more like my interest in things got lower and this heavy fatigue settled in and didn’t really lift the way I expected it to. So… not six months or longer, but definitely a few months. Maybe around three.

inference.note: Duration of about 3 months argues against classic chronic fatigue syndrome criteria requiring 6+ months, lowering G93.3 but not fully excluding a fatigue-related syndrome. Low interest and weighed-down mood keep depressive disorders in consideration; medical causes like E03.9 remain possible.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is depressed mood most of the day, a key discriminator between a major depressive episode/dysthymia and primarily fatigue-related or medical causes.
doctor.question: For the past few months, have you felt sad or down most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about depressed mood—feeling sad or down most of the day nearly every day—but the provided symptom profile does not include a distinct depressed mood item.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve definitely felt… low, I guess, or kind of weighed down at times, but “sad most of the day nearly every day” feels harder for me to say yes to.

It’s not like I’m crying all day or constantly thinking, “I’m sad.” A lot of the time it’s more like I feel flat, or slowed down, or just not very bright inside, if that makes sense. But then there are also parts of the day where I’m distracted or just going through the motions, and I don’t know if that counts as feeling sad or not.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say it’s been clearly sad all day every day, but something has definitely felt off emotionally for the past few months.

doctor.intent: Assess anhedonia to distinguish a depressive episode from primarily fatigue-related or medical causes.
doctor.question: Over the past few months, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I stopped caring about the things that usually make me feel like myself, like sketching, going to gallery openings, cooking, yoga, or even playing tennis with a friend.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether interest or pleasure in usually enjoyable activities has decreased over the past few months.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, I think that’s probably the clearest part of it, honestly. I’ve sort of stopped caring about the things that usually make me feel like me.

Like, I used to sketch pretty regularly—not necessarily anything amazing, just little studies or ideas in a notebook—and normally that feels grounding. But lately the sketchbook just sits there, and I’ll look at it and think I should want to pick it up, but I don’t. Same with going to gallery openings. That used to be something I’d actually get excited about, even just getting dressed and wandering around and seeing what people were making. Now it feels like this whole effort, and I can’t really imagine enjoying it once I’m there.

Cooking has been like that too. I used to like trying recipes or making something nice for myself, and now it’s more like… I don’t care enough. Yoga feels similar. And even tennis with a friend, which should be fun and social and active, just doesn’t pull me in the way it normally would.

So, yes. It’s not that I hate those things now, exactly. It’s more like the part of me that used to feel interested or pleased by them has gotten really quiet.

inference.note: Anhedonia over ~3 months increases likelihood of a depressive episode (F32.9) and keeps recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9) in play pending past episodes. Duration under 2 years argues against F34.1 as primary but not enough to fully rule it out yet. Fatigue >6 months criterion not met, making G93.3 less likely though still possible early/partial picture; E03.9 remains a medical rule-out for fatigue/low mood.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a distinct change in appetite, which helps assess for a current major depressive episode versus other causes of fatigue.
doctor.question: Over the past few months, has your appetite changed?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: My appetite has been off enough that I sometimes realize I’ve only had coffee and a few bites all day, and my jeans have gotten looser without me trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about changes in appetite over the past few months.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it has. Not in a dramatic way where I’m, like, deliberately not eating or anything, but my appetite has been pretty off.

Some days I’ll get to later in the afternoon and realize I’ve basically only had coffee and maybe a few bites of something—like half a piece of toast or a couple forkfuls of leftovers—and I didn’t even really notice I was skipping meals. Food just doesn’t sound that appealing, or it feels like too much effort to decide what to eat.

And I have noticed my jeans are looser. I wasn’t trying to lose weight, so that kind of stood out to me. It’s not something I was aiming for; it just sort of happened along with not eating very much some days.

doctor.intent: Assess suicidal ideation to help distinguish a major depressive episode from other causes of fatigue and low energy, and for safety.
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal thoughts or self-harm, which is not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I’ve had clear thoughts like, “I’m going to hurt myself,” if that’s what you mean. And I don’t have, like, a plan or anything I’m sitting with.

But the “life isn’t worth living” part is harder, because sometimes when I’m really low or just worn out, I’ll have this kind of vague feeling of, “What is the point of doing all of this?” Not in a dramatic way, more like this heavy, exhausted thought that everything feels like too much. Then it passes, or I distract myself, or I just sort of keep going.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t been actively trying to hurt myself. But I have had those darker, pointless-feeling thoughts around the edges sometimes, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Assess psychomotor retardation, a key neurovegetative symptom that would strengthen major depressive episode over medical fatigue syndromes or neurasthenia.
doctor.question: Have you been moving or speaking more slowly than usual lately?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: On my slower days, it feels like my body is moving through wet cement, and even answering a simple question from my spouse can take me a weirdly long time.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about slowed movement or speech, which directly matches psychomotor slowing/changes.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not every single day, but on the slower days it’s pretty noticeable to me.

It’s like my body is moving through wet cement, if that makes sense. I’ll be doing something basic, like getting up from the couch or walking to the kitchen, and everything just feels heavier and slower than it should. Not painful, exactly, just like there’s this delay between deciding to move and actually moving.

And talking can feel that way too. My spouse will ask me something simple, like what I want to do or whether I need anything, and I’ll just sit there for a weirdly long time trying to answer. I can tell it’s taking too long, which makes me feel awkward, but it’s like the words don’t come out right away. I’m not trying to ignore them. It’s more like everything in me is lagging.

inference.note: Current symptoms over ~3 months include anhedonia, decreased appetite/weight loss, psychomotor slowing, fatigue, and passive death thoughts, which increases likelihood of a depressive episode and makes G93.3 less likely because duration is <6 months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are physical symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism rather than a primary depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually sensitive to cold lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unusual sensitivity to cold, which is not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

Um… unusually sensitive to cold? I don’t think so. I mean, I get cold sometimes, but not in a way that’s stood out to me as different or weird.

Like, I’ll put on a sweatshirt if the house is chilly, but I haven’t been thinking, “Why am I freezing all the time?” or anything like that. I guess I haven’t really been tracking it closely, but no, nothing noticeable comes to mind.

inference.note: E03.9 is less likely after the patient denied unusual cold sensitivity. Depressive disorders remain favored given ~3 months of anhedonia, appetite/weight loss, psychomotor slowing, fatigue, and passive death thoughts. F34.1 is less likely because duration is only about 3 months, but kept as a residual candidate pending full episode history. F48.0 remains possible due to prominent fatigue/nonrestorative sleep but is less favored than depression.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ever had a past major depressive episode, which would distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder from a single current episode and from persistent depressive disorder/neurasthenia.
doctor.question: Before this started about three months ago, have you ever had another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in things most days?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any prior depressive episodes before the current three-month period, and the symptom profile only describes the current depressive symptoms/duration, not past episodes.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I’ve had low stretches before, like times where I felt really discouraged or kind of flat, but I don’t know if I could say it was a full two weeks most days, if that makes sense.

I’m trying to think back, and it all gets a little blurry because I don’t usually mark it on a calendar or anything. I can remember bad days, or maybe a bad week here and there, but whether it was really depressed or not interested in things nearly every day for two weeks… I don’t know that I can confidently say yes.

So I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not sure. Nothing as clear in my memory as, “that was definitely a two-week period.”

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there was a prior major depressive episode, which best separates recurrent major depressive disorder from a single depressive episode and the chronic alternatives.
doctor.question: Before this current stretch, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether there was a prior lifetime episode before the current stretch lasting at least two weeks with depressed mood or loss of interest. The symptom profile only describes the current depressive episode and does not cover prior episodes.

patient.answer:
I know you just asked that in a slightly different way, and I’m trying not to over-answer it, but… I really don’t know.

Before this current stretch, I’ve definitely had times where I felt down or kind of emotionally shut off, like I wasn’t as interested in things as I normally would be. But when you say nearly every day for at least two weeks, that’s the part I can’t honestly pin down. I can remember patches of feeling bad, but I don’t know if they lasted that long or if it was more like a few bad days mixed in with some okay days.

I don’t want to say yes just because I’ve had rough periods, if that makes sense. This one feels more clear to me because it’s recent and I’ve been aware of it. The older stuff is just harder for me to sort out. So… maybe there were times like that, but I’m not confident enough to say there definitely were.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ever had a manic or hypomanic episode, which would rule against unipolar depressive disorders and most strongly separates the remaining candidates.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or irritable for several days in a row?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For weeks I felt unusually lit up and sure everything was going to be amazing, but I could also snap at my husband over small comments about the budget or the house.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a period of unusually high, energized, or irritable mood lasting several days, which directly matches elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, I think so. There have been times where for weeks I felt almost, I don’t know, lit up. Like everything suddenly seemed possible and I was completely sure things were about to be amazing, even if nothing had really changed enough to explain why I felt that way.

And it wasn’t just being in a good mood for a day or two. It felt bigger than that, like I had this energy or excitement running through me. But at the same time, I could get really touchy. My husband would make some small comment about the budget, or something around the house, and I’d just snap at him like he had said something terrible. Then later I’d think, why did I react that strongly?

So yes, there have been periods like that, and they lasted more than several days. More like weeks, at least the ones I’m thinking of.

inference.note: New history of multi-day to multi-week periods of elevated/energized or irritable mood raises bipolar spectrum disorder, so bipolar candidates are added. Pure dysthymia/neurasthenia are less likely and removed given current major depressive symptoms plus possible past hypomanic/manic episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated periods included decreased need for sleep, which would help distinguish bipolar spectrum illness from unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During those weeks when you felt lit up, did you need less sleep than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about decreased need for sleep during an elevated/energized period, but the provided symptom profile does not include a decreased-need-for-sleep item.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure, honestly. I’m trying to think about those weeks specifically, and I don’t have a clean memory of, like, “Oh yes, I was only sleeping three hours and felt fine,” or anything that clear.

I do remember feeling more awake or keyed up in general during those times, but whether I actually needed less sleep than usual… I don’t know. I might have stayed up later some nights because I felt like my mind was still going, but I can’t confidently say my sleep was dramatically reduced or that I didn’t feel tired afterward.

So I guess the honest answer is: maybe a little, but I didn’t track it, and it’s not one of the things I remember clearly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated periods included abnormally increased goal-directed activity, which would support a hypomanic/manic episode and help distinguish bipolar disorder from major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: During those weeks when you felt lit up, were you more driven than usual to start or do a lot of projects or activities?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I started contacting galleries, drafting newsletter sections, planning community workshops, and trying to line up freelance clients all at once, which was way more than I could actually follow through on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the elevated/irritable weeks, I became unusually driven to start or do many projects or activities, which directly matches increased goal-directed activity.

patient.answer:
Yes. That part I remember pretty clearly, actually. I would suddenly feel like I had this whole plan for my life and I needed to act on all of it immediately.

Like, I started contacting galleries, and I was drafting sections for a newsletter, and then I was planning these community workshop ideas, and at the same time trying to line up freelance clients. It wasn’t just one project where I was excited and focused — it was like five different directions at once, and they all felt urgent and totally realistic in the moment.

Looking back, it was way more than I could actually follow through on. I’d start making lists and sending emails and sketching out plans, and I’d feel like, “Okay, this is it, I’m finally getting everything moving.” But then there was just too much happening, and a lot of it didn’t really get finished or went nowhere because I had taken on more than I could manage. So yes, definitely more driven than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included grandiosity/inflated self-esteem, which would help distinguish bipolar I/II spectrum from unipolar depression and clarify whether the episode was hypomanic/manic rather than just improved mood.
doctor.question: During those weeks when you felt lit up, did you feel more confident or powerful than usual?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I honestly believed I could turn the newsletter, a gallery partnership, and a consulting business into something big almost overnight, even though I hadn’t really worked out the basics.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the energized period, the patient felt unusually confident or powerful, which directly matches inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Yes, I did. I don’t think I would have called it “powerful” at the time, because that sounds so dramatic, but… I definitely felt unusually sure of myself. Like I had finally figured out something everyone else hadn’t, or like I was suddenly capable of making these huge things happen if I just pushed hard enough.

I remember honestly believing I could take the newsletter idea, get a gallery partnership going, and turn that into some kind of consulting business or bigger professional thing almost overnight. And I mean, looking back, I hadn’t really worked out the basics. I didn’t have a clear business plan, or enough contacts, or even a realistic sense of how all of it would actually function. But at the time it didn’t feel unrealistic. It felt obvious, like, “Of course I can do this. Why wouldn’t this work?”

It wasn’t just normal confidence, I guess. It was more like this certainty that I was on the edge of something big and that I could pull it all together faster than anyone would expect. I felt kind of unstoppable in that way, even though now I can see there were a lot of missing pieces.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods caused marked impairment or hospitalization, which best distinguishes bipolar I from bipolar II/unspecified bipolar disorder and from depressive disorders.
doctor.question: During those weeks when you felt lit up, did that cause serious problems in your life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve fallen behind in my certificate coursework and let bills, meals, and household tasks pile up because I can’t keep my plans organized or follow through consistently. My spouse has had to step in more at home, and I’ve pulled back from friends and art commitments I normally care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the lit-up weeks caused serious life problems, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it catastrophic, but it definitely caused problems. More than I wanted to admit at the time.

The biggest thing is that I couldn’t actually keep everything organized. I’d have all these plans and ideas and I’d be starting things, but the normal stuff in my life started slipping. I fell behind in my certificate coursework because I kept thinking I was going to catch up later, or I’d sit down to do it and get pulled into some other plan that felt more urgent. And then suddenly I was behind enough that it felt embarrassing to even look at it.

At home, things piled up too. Bills, meals, basic household tasks — not because I didn’t care, but because I was just not following through consistently. I’d have these bursts where I thought I was going to reorganize everything, and then somehow the actual practical things didn’t get done. My spouse had to step in more, and I feel bad about that because it wasn’t fair. It put more on them.

And socially, I kind of pulled back from people and from art commitments I normally really care about. Which is strange, because I felt like I was doing all these big important things, but in reality I was dropping the regular things and relationships that keep me steady.

So yes, it did cause problems. I guess “serious” depends how you define it, but it affected my schoolwork, my home life, and my relationships enough that I can’t really say it was just harmless energy.

inference.note: History now supports a bipolar spectrum disorder: prior multi-week episodes of elevated/irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity, inflated confidence, and clear functional impairment, while current symptoms are a depressive episode. This makes unipolar depressive disorders (F32.9, F33.9) less likely and rules them out from the candidate list. Hypomanic/manic symptoms are evident, but duration/sleep change/hospitalization/psychosis are not fully clarified, so F31.8 and F31.9 remain.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods met the duration threshold for a manic episode versus hypomania, to distinguish bipolar I disorder from other bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Did any of those unusually energized or lit-up periods last at least one full week?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For weeks I felt unusually lit up and sure everything was going to be amazing, but I could also snap at my husband over small comments about the budget or the house.
target_item.reason: The question asks about the duration of the unusually energized or lit-up mood period, which most directly relates to the elevated or irritable mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yes. It wasn’t just a day or two where I was in a good mood or had a burst of motivation. It lasted for weeks at a time, that kind of lit-up feeling where everything seemed exciting and possible and like it was all about to turn into something amazing.

I remember being really sure of myself during those stretches, like things were finally clicking and I just had to keep moving with it. But it wasn’t only upbeat, exactly. I could get irritable too, especially at home. If my husband made a small comment about the budget or the house, things that were probably reasonable to bring up, I’d snap at him like he was trying to slow me down or criticize me. At the time it felt like he was being negative, but looking back, my reaction was bigger than the comment deserved.

So yes, definitely at least a full week. More like several weeks, from what I remember.

inference.note: At least one week of elevated/irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity/confidence, and functional impairment supports a bipolar spectrum disorder and keeps bipolar I/other specified bipolar as leading possibilities; lack of clear evidence yet for hospitalization/psychosis or enough specific manic symptoms to definitively distinguish them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included psychotic features, which would support bipolar I disorder rather than bipolar II disorder/other bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: During those lit-up periods, did you ever have beliefs that other people said were clearly untrue or unrealistic?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I honestly believed I could turn the newsletter, a gallery partnership, and a consulting business into something big almost overnight, even though I hadn’t really worked out the basics.
target_item.reason: The question asks about unrealistic or clearly untrue beliefs during lit-up periods, which most directly relates to grandiosity or inflated self-esteem.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not like I believed something completely impossible in a bizarre way, but I definitely believed things that other people thought were unrealistic. At the time, I didn’t experience them as unrealistic at all.

The main one was this whole idea that I could take the newsletter I was working on, connect it with a gallery partnership, and somehow turn that into a consulting business or this much bigger professional thing almost immediately. Like, almost overnight, in my mind. I was talking about it as if it was just a matter of pushing hard enough and making the right moves, and then it would all fall into place.

And people around me were kind of trying to point out that I hadn’t really figured out the basics. I didn’t have a real plan, or enough contacts, or a clear sense of how the money would work, or what I was actually offering. But when they said that, I remember feeling like they just didn’t understand the scale of it yet. Like they were being too cautious or small-minded.

Looking back, it feels embarrassing, because there were so many steps missing. But at the time, I honestly believed I could make it into something big very quickly, and I was really certain about it.

inference.note: This turn established psychotic features during a manic episode: elevated/irritable mood lasting weeks, increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity, functional impairment, and unrealistic fixed beliefs. This narrows bipolar disorder to a manic episode with psychotic symptoms rather than other bipolar spectrum options.
